strengths: Novel hybrid-thinking framework: The adaptive switching between text-based and tool-based M-CoT is well-motivated and, to the authors' knowledge, first proposed for autonomous driving decision-making. This elegantly balances efficiency and reliability.

Principled three-stage progressive training strategy: The progression from foundation-building (DM-SFT) → mode-strengthening (FCM-RL) → autonomous selection (AMS-RL) is systematic and well-designed. Ablations convincingly demonstrate each stage's contribution.

Comprehensive evaluation methodology: Multiple complementary metrics (accuracy, H-Score, MSA) capture different aspects of performance. The MSA metric for evaluating mode selection appropriateness is novel and useful.

Strong experimental results: Achieves 70.11% first-frame and 44.06% sequence-average accuracy, substantial improvements over the best baseline (36.51% and 38.54% respectively). The ablation study effectively validates design choices.

Well-motivated vision toolkit: The four tools (high-res view retrieval, RoI inspection, depth estimation, 3D detection) are grounded in human driving behavior and clearly specified with proper implementation details.

Thorough ablations on progressive training and active perception: Table 2 and 3 provide compelling evidence that each component is necessary. The dramatic 43.1% drop when removing images demonstrates genuine visual grounding.

Clear presentation and solid technical execution: The paper is generally well-written with good motivation, clear methodology, and comprehensive appendix with reward formulas and implementation details.
weaknesses: Evaluation limited to single dataset (SUP-AD): This is a significant limitation for generalization claims. Multi-dataset evaluation (e.g., nuScenes, Waymo, CARLA simulation) would substantially strengthen the paper. A top-tier venue typically expects broader evaluation.

Unfair baseline comparisons: Proprietary models (Claude, GPT-4.1, Gemini) are evaluated with one-shot prompting without any task-specific training, while DriveAgent-R1 receives extensive training on SUP-AD data. The claim of 'outperforming even leading proprietary models' is misleading without proper caveat. Fair comparison would require training baselines on the same data or using established benchmarks.

Insufficient analysis of mode selection failures: MSA of 65.93% means ~34% incorrect selections, but there's minimal analysis of failure cases. Which scenarios cause wrong mode selection? When should tool-based reasoning be used but isn't? Case studies would strengthen claims about adaptive selection.

No inference latency analysis: Tool invocation has computational cost, but no timing analysis is provided. Is 3 tool calls per trajectory practical for real-time driving? This is critical for real-world deployment.

Limited tool utility analysis: No ablation on individual tools or sensitivity analysis on the 3-call limit. Which tools are most helpful? How does performance degrade with fewer calls? The vision toolkit design appears somewhat ad-hoc.

Incomplete interpretability analysis: Despite emphasizing interpretability through structured CoT, the paper provides few qualitative examples comparing text-based vs. tool-based reasoning. The H-Score relies on external evaluator (Gemini) reliability. How different is reasoning quality between modes?

Reward function complexity without sensitivity analysis: Multiple hyperparameters (w_speed, w_traj, w_fmt, curriculum bounds θ_lower, θ_upper) but no sensitivity analysis. The oracle-based data construction (72B model) could introduce systematic bias—no validation that oracle judgments are correct.
Training data scale concerns: Only 5K SFT samples (2.5K per mode). How much improvement comes from the small, curated dataset vs. the methodology itself? Unclear if results scale with more data.
Reproducibility issues: Code not released, complex three-stage training pipeline, proprietary vision tools, potential limited access to SUP-AD dataset. External readers would struggle to reproduce.

Generalization unexplored: No cross-dataset evaluation, no CARLA simulation, no analysis of robustness to different environments or VLM backbones. How does this scale to other autonomous driving settings?

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing myopic decision-making and passive perception in VLM-based driving agents
Thoughtful three-stage progressive training strategy (DM-SFT → FCM-RL → AMS-RL) with clear pedagogical progression
Practical and well-designed vision toolkit with tools grounded in human driving behavior (high-res view retrieval, RoI inspection, depth estimation, 3D detection)
Comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 2-3) that validate individual components and visual grounding
Clear technical presentation with informative figures demonstrating the hybrid-thinking and reasoning process
Multi-dimensional evaluation combining accuracy, holistic scores, and mode selection accuracy metrics
weaknesses: Fundamentally unfair baseline comparisons: DriveAgent-R1 is extensively trained (5K SFT + RL) while SOTA models are evaluated in one-shot setting, making the 70.11% vs 30.03% gap misleading and primarily attributable to training advantage rather than algorithmic superiority

Severely limited evaluation scope: single dataset (SUP-AD) only with 1,500 test samples; no generalization analysis to other datasets (nuScenes, Waymo, CARLA) or diverse scenarios raises serious overfitting concerns

Unclear contribution attribution: Table 2 shows most gains come from RL stages; MSA of 65.93% indicates the model fails optimal mode selection 34% of the time, undermining hybrid-thinking value proposition

Missing critical analysis of tool usage: no quantification of when/why tools are invoked, no strategic use patterns analyzed, no robustness testing against tool failures despite relying on oracle implementations of Depth Anything V2 and 3D detection in practice

Data construction pipeline issues: relies on 72B teacher model to generate training data for 3B student, creating bias and data leakage; inverse reasoning from ground truth is artificial and may not reflect natural reasoning patterns

Vision toolkit deployment gap: assumes perfect tool implementations (depth estimation, 3D detection) that will have errors in real-world scenarios; no robustness analysis against inevitable tool failures
Insufficient active perception validation: Table 3 conflates tool capability with training effects; cleaner experiment would train identical models with/without tool access at inference time

Limited novelty in individual components: hybrid reasoning, tool-use in VLMs, and toolkit elements all draw from existing work (Visual Sketchpad, AgentThink, existing detection tools); main contribution is the training strategy which is somewhat incremental
Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple runs reported; results could be within noise margins
Missing key implementation details: computational cost, inference latency with tool calls, and practical accessibility of 72B model for cold-start data generation not discussed

strengths: Novel hybrid-thinking framework that adaptively switches between text-based and tool-based reasoning, well-motivated for autonomous driving
Comprehensive system design with four complementary vision tools (high-res retrieval, RoI inspection, depth estimation, 3D detection)
Strong experimental results on SUP-AD: 70.11% first-frame accuracy with tools, exceeding one-shot proprietary VLMs
Thorough ablation studies validating each training stage and demonstrating visual grounding (43.1% accuracy drop without images)
Well-structured three-stage progressive training strategy (DM-SFT → FCM-RL → AMS-RL) with clear motivation
Clear presentation with effective figures (especially Figs. 1-3) and detailed methodology appendix
Comprehensive evaluation metrics (ACC, H-Score, Mode Selection Accuracy)
weaknesses: Critical limitation: evaluation on only a single dataset (SUP-AD with 1,500 test samples); no cross-dataset validation on NUSCENES, Waymo, BDD100K, or other benchmarks; severely limits generalization claims

Unfair baseline comparisons: all proprietary models evaluated one-shot without task-specific training while DriveAgent-R1 undergoes three stages of extensive training; missing comparison with other trained driving agents (e.g., trained AlphaDrive, DriveVLM)

Incremental novelty: hybrid reasoning, tool-based M-CoT, and three-stage training are existing paradigms; main contribution is engineering their combination for driving rather than fundamental innovation

Insufficient active perception analysis: no ablation of individual tool contributions; vision toolkit uses standard techniques with limited novelty; conflation of 'vision input availability' with 'effective tool use' in Table 3

Mode selection suboptimal: free-choice mode (70.11%) significantly underperforms oracle (71.23%); no qualitative analysis or failure cases; MSA metric is somewhat circular; missing examples of mode selection reasoning
Modest long-horizon capability: only predicts 4 meta-actions over 8 seconds, which is short-term tactical planning; unclear multi-step plan coherence
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multi-run results; single test split without stability analysis
Insufficient error analysis: no discussion of failure modes, only one qualitative example (Fig. 1), missing analysis of tool accuracy propagation and when hybrid approach fails
Evaluation limitations: single-keyframe only (not closed-loop video), H-Score depends on external Gemini 2.5 evaluator, no safety metrics or real-world validation, no computational cost analysis

Data construction complexity: multiple-stage pipeline (Fig. 4) prone to implementation drift; small SFT dataset (5K samples); inverse reasoning from ground truth may generate unrealistically easy data
Scalability unclear: uses 3B base model; unclear how approach scales to larger VLMs or whether claimed superiority holds with properly trained larger models
Reproducibility concerns: vision toolkit integration details missing, no code release announced, exact RL iteration counts not specified

strengths: Strong empirical results: 3B model achieves competitive performance with GPT-5 and human drivers on autonomous driving planning task
Rigorous experimental methodology: comprehensive ablations, multiple baselines (closed-source and open-source models), human evaluation, and cross-dataset validation
Well-designed hybrid-thinking framework: sensible integration of efficient text-based and robust tool-augmented reasoning with clear motivation from human cognition
Technically sound approach: Mode-Partitioned GRPO (MP-GRPO) enables multi-dimensional contrastive learning; sophisticated reward design with position-action weighting for class imbalance
Transparent and reproducible: extensive appendix with implementation details, prompts, data construction pipelines, and honest discussion of limitations and failure cases
Practical efficiency benefits: 20% latency reduction compared to passive approaches while maintaining competitive accuracy
Active perception for planning is novel in autonomous driving context: demonstrates that tools can effectively ground decisions in visual evidence when properly trained
weaknesses: Limited novelty: active perception via tool-augmented CoT is incremental extension of existing multimodal chain-of-thought literature; hybrid reasoning and mixture-of-experts selection are well-established; main contribution is domain-specific application rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation

Dataset and reproducibility concerns: Drive-Internal is proprietary/internal dataset limiting independent validation; substantial performance gap between Drive-Internal (51.34%) and nuScenes (47.10%) suggests distribution shift; test sets relatively small (1.5K and 2K examples); meta-action labels depend on GPT-4 refinement with unknown label quality

Low mode selection accuracy undermines core contribution: Mode Selection Accuracy only reaches 45.42%, meaning model fails to select optimal mode ~55% of the time; adaptive mode accuracy (45.42%) is comparable to or lower than forced modes, questioning the value of hybrid thinking

Critical safety limitation not adequately addressed: acknowledged over-reliance on tool outputs (Section 6.11) where agent can be misled by new visual evidence; failure case shows agent incorrectly switching from correct green light decision to stop based on seeing red pedestrian light; proposed solutions (stronger domain alignment) are vague and untested

Evaluation lacks rigor: no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; human baseline from only 3 drivers with each evaluating 1/3 of samples (no inter-rater agreement); comparison with closed-source models via 'no-thinking mode' may not be optimal; no closed-loop simulation or real-world validation; no error analysis by scenario complexity or action frequency

Technical design choices not fully justified: max 3 tool calls has no ablation; Rtool reward uses constant per-tool cost despite tools having different computational costs (Retrieve View << 3D Object Detection); MSA metric is circular (optimal mode defined post-hoc using test-set accuracy); FCM-RL necessity before AMS-RL not convincingly demonstrated

Limited scope: only high-level behavioral planning (4 discrete actions over 8 seconds); no low-level motion planning; only front-view as default input; no evaluation on extreme conditions (severe weather, night driving, adversarial scenarios)

Generalization concerns: evaluation limited to two datasets with specific characteristics; performance gap between datasets is substantial; no zero-shot or few-shot transfer; no out-of-distribution evaluation; unclear how performance scales with scene complexity or action rarity
